title: The Entryway
subtitle: The entryway is the smallest room in the house and the one that sets the tone for every other. This playbook points the whole 6S loop at it, one small zone at a time, and it does not stop at telling you what to do: for every zone it gives you the exact inputs to gather and the precise, step-by-step way to clean and shine it to a professional standard, so the door does not just get tidy, it gets genuinely, inspectably clean.
part_position: FIRST chapter of Part Nine (Room-by-Room Playbooks), and the OPENING chapter of the applied half of the book. The six-S method (Parts 1 to 8, the full six-S journey) is complete; Part Nine points the finished loop at one real room at a time. This is the FIRST of twenty room playbooks (Chapters 31 to 50, one per room in the Micro Zone Manual), and the PROOF chapter that establishes the new Part 9 format. The CORE of the format, and of this chapter, is the detailed, step-by-step clean-and-shine instruction for each micro-zone, with the exact inputs to gather, governed by a universal nine-rule Shine method. It follows Chapter 30 (Your Next 6S Event), the finale of the main arc, and hands off to Chapter 32 (The Kitchen). The friction meter, which reached its goal at Chapter 30, is RETIRED for Part 9 and replaced by a BEFORE-AND-AFTER room signature

hands_off_note: Chapter 31 opens Part Nine and is the first of twenty room playbooks. Its whole work is to prove the new applied format: the teaching stops and the doing begins. The reader now owns all six S's and the loop that keeps them turning, so a playbook does not re-teach Sort or Shine; it takes the room you are standing in, breaks it into the handful of small zones it is really made of, and, for each zone, gives the exact inputs to gather and the exact, ordered, step-by-step way to clean and shine it, done the way a professional would rather than the way most of us wipe at a surface until it looks a bit better. That distinction is the whole game: a tidy room and a genuinely clean room are not the same thing, and the difference is method. It BEGINS AT THE DOOR, and not by accident: the entryway is the room you cross most and notice most, and it is also the dirtiest room in the house for its size, because it is where the outside comes in (grit, road salt, rain, everything that rides in on shoes and sleeves), which is exactly why the clean-and-shine step matters most here and why the chapter spends most of its length on precisely how to do it. It delivers the single most freeing idea in the applied half of the book, FIVE ZONES, NOT ONE ROOM (you do not 6S a whole room, you 6S one zone of it, then the next; the entryway is five small zones, the landing spot, the coats, the shoes, the bench or console, and the door with its mat and the strip of floor inside its swing) with the rule and the five-zones line. It runs THE QUICK PASSES briskly (Sort each zone first because you cannot clean a surface that is covered; Straighten survivors into a home chosen by use; Safety, Standardize, and Sustain, each short, after the shine) and then slows right down for SHINE, teaching the universal NINE-RULE SHINE METHOD once (top to bottom; dry before wet; back to front, clean to dirty; mist the cloth not the surface; two cloths, one to clean and one to dry; colour-code cloths and never use fabric softener; match the cleaner to the surface; give the cleaner a moment to work; clean to inspect and flag, do not fix) with the Shine method line. Its CENTERPIECE is ZONE BY ZONE: EXACTLY HOW TO CLEAN IT, which gives every zone the same three things, the exact INPUTS to gather into the caddy, the NUMBERED steps in the true order of work (clear and unplug, dust high and dry, glass, surfaces, details, floor last), and an INSPECT-AND-FLAG list, because Shine finds the hazards and the safety pass fixes them. It lands the definition box (a finished entryway is one where everyone can land and launch in seconds). It names THE CALLS THAT MATTER HERE (the paper with no verdict, the guilty coat counted by weather, the tired mat you test rather than look at) with the count-by-weather and worn-mat reframes. It runs WATCH FOR AT THE DOOR (the room's hazards through the five safety questions, where the safety pass fixes everything the clean flagged). And it closes with the Part 9 SIGNATURE that replaces the friction meter, the BEFORE-AND-AFTER pair and the two photos to take (the before kept, the after taped inside the cupboard as the standard), before a light hand-off to Chapter 32 (The Kitchen). It does NOT re-teach the six S's; it points the loop the reader already owns at their first real room, and shows them precisely how to clean it.
audience: Readers who have completed the whole six-S method (Parts 1 to 8) and now want to apply it. They have learned to sort by belonging and need, to give everything a home chosen by use, to clean in a way that inspects, to protect the people first, to write down the best way they know, and to keep it all alive with a daily rhythm and a periodic event, and at Chapter 30 the friction meter reached its goal. Busy home keepers and parents. They do not need Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, or Sustain re-taught; they need somewhere to point what they have learned, and a set of instructions precise enough to follow with their sleeves rolled up: the exact inputs to gather and the exact, ordered steps to clean and shine each zone to a professional standard. The danger for this audience is two-fold: overwhelm, looking at a whole entryway as one big undifferentiated job and stalling; and settling for tidy rather than genuinely clean. The chapter removes the first by turning the room into a short list of finishable zones, and the second by teaching a real cleaning method. The register is warm, capable, and a little celebratory: this is where the reader gets to spend the method they worked to build, so the feeling is capability, not instruction, you already know how, now clean a real room to a standard. No shame about the before state; the before photo is honoured, not mocked. No hype, no force. The emotional heart is capability and quiet delight at a real room becoming genuinely, inspectably clean.
core_promise: Point the finished six-S loop at your first real room and clean it to a professional standard, not just tidy it. Stop seeing a room and start seeing zones: you do not 6S a whole entryway, you 6S one of its five small zones, then the next, the landing spot, the coats, the shoes, the bench or console, and the door with its mat and the strip of floor inside its swing, each a job you can finish in an afternoon. Learn the universal nine-rule Shine method once (work top to bottom, dry before wet, back to front and clean to dirty, mist the cloth not the surface, two cloths one to clean and one to dry, colour-code your cloths and never use fabric softener, match the cleaner to the surface, give the cleaner a moment to work, and clean to inspect and flag, do not fix) and then apply it zone by zone, with the exact inputs to gather and the exact numbered steps in the true order of work. Clean to inspect: your hand passes over every surface, so your eye should too, flagging the frayed cord, loose bracket, or soft patch of rot as you go, because Shine finds the hazard and the safety pass fixes it. Make the entryway's three hardest calls: the paper (every sheet gets a verdict; a sheet past fourteen days is a decision, not paperwork), the guilty coat (count by weather, not by number), and the tired mat (test it, do not look at it). And take the before-and-after pair that keeps the room the way you just made it: the before kept as proof, the after taped inside the cupboard as the standard the door has to match. A finished entryway is one where everyone can land and launch in seconds, and every surface is genuinely, inspectably clean.

The feeling it should leave is capability rather than instruction, you already know how, so here is precisely how to clean a real room to a professional standard under the loop you own. It must honour the before state without mocking it, the before photo is kept and honoured, not laughed at, and it must never imply the room must be conquered in one exhausting go, because the whole point is that a room is a short list of finishable jobs and one zone cleaned properly beats five wiped-at ones. No shame, no force, no hype, no discipline-as-punishment language (no no excuses, stay disciplined, make yourself, hold the line), no hype words (unlock, leverage, elevate, supercharge, optimize, 10x), no brand names and no named systems. The friction meter reached its goal at Chapter 30 and is retired for Part 9; its recurring-close role is taken by the before-and-after room signature, so each room gets its own concrete transformation as the emotional payoff.
practical_purpose: Teach the reader to decompose the entryway into its five zones, and, for each zone, to clean and shine it to a professional standard with the exact inputs and the exact steps, without re-teaching the six S's. Establish the room-as-zones principle: a whole room feels like too much because you are looking at it as one big undifferentiated job; it is a small collection of separate zones that share a name and a bit of floor, and the trick to all of Part 9 is to stop seeing the room and start seeing the zones, each with a clear edge and a clear finish. Then, as the centerpiece, walk zone by zone, giving each the same three parts: the INPUTS to gather into the caddy, the NUMBERED steps in the true order of work, and the INSPECT-AND-FLAG list. hero_device: The room as micro-zones, cleaned to a method (point the finished loop at one room, one zone at a time, and clean each zone to a professional standard). A room is not one big job but a handful of small, finishable zones wearing a single name; you run the six S's through each zone, and the deep, detailed part, the part this chapter is really about, is Shine. The rule: you do not 6S a whole room, you 6S one zone of it, then the next, until the room is done; a room is only ever a handful of small zones wearing a single name, and a zone is a job you can finish in an afternoon. Applied to the entryway, that is five zones: the landing spot, the coats, the shoes, the bench or console, and the door with its mat and the strip of floor inside its swing. The centerpiece, and the thing that makes this a playbook rather than a lesson, is that for each zone the chapter gives the exact inputs to gather and the exact, ordered, numbered steps to clean and shine it, governed by the universal nine-rule Shine method
secondary_device: The universal nine-rule Shine method, taught once and applied in every zone and every room. Shine is where a room stops being tidy and becomes clean, and it is the pass most people do worst because they were never taught a method. The nine rules: work top to bottom; work dry before wet; work back to front, clean to dirty; mist the cloth, not the surface; use two cloths, one to clean and one to dry; colour-code your cloths and never use fabric softener; match the cleaner to the surface; give the cleaner a moment to work; and clean to inspect, and flag, do not fix. Every zone procedure in the chapter is just these nine rules applied to a particular surface, with the same handful of inputs. Paired with the before-and-after room signature, the Part 9 device that replaces the friction meter: when the five zones are done and cleaned to the method, stand where you stood at the start, just inside the door, and take the second photograph, a true matched pair, the before kept as proof and the after taped inside the cupboard as the standard the door has to match
shine_method: Shine is cleaning to a method, not wiping until it looks better: work top to bottom and dry before wet, mist the cloth and not the surface, clean with one cloth and dry with a second, and let your eye inspect every surface your hand passes over. You leave the zone genuinely clean, and you find what needs fixing on the way. This universal method is stated once and governs every zone-by-zone procedure in the chapter and across all twenty room playbooks. CRITICAL: Shine NOTICES and FLAGS hazards (frayed cords, loose brackets, rot, rust); FIXING belongs to the Safety pass. Shine finds it; the safety pass fixes it.

nine_shine_rules_note: The nine best-practice rules the Shine method rests on, given verbatim as bolded rules in the manuscript's How to Shine the Entryway section: Work top to bottom (clean the highest surface first and the floor last, so dust and drips fall onto what you have not cleaned yet). Work dry before wet (dust or vacuum loose grit before anything wet, because a damp cloth over dry grit makes mud and scratches the finish). Work back to front, clean to dirty (start at the back edge and pull toward you, least dirty to dirtiest, so you never drag grime across clean ground or walk over a wet floor). Mist the cloth, not the surface (spray the cleaner onto the cloth, so nothing runs down behind a frame and no overspray lands where it should not). Use two cloths, one to clean and one to dry (a surface left wet air-dries to streaks, and a wet floor at a doorway is a fall waiting to happen). Colour-code your cloths (a dedicated colour for glass, another for general surfaces, another for the floor and boot tray, washed by colour and never with fabric softener, which clogs the fibres and kills their grab). Match the cleaner to the surface (neutral pH multi-surface cleaner for sealed surfaces, streak-free glass cleaner for glass and mirror, a floor cleaner matched to your floor material). Give the cleaner a moment to work (let it sit on a sticky mark rather than scrubbing it dry). Clean to inspect, and flag, do not fix (your hand passes over every inch, so your eye should too; note or flag the frayed cord, loose bracket, or soft patch of rot and keep cleaning; Shine finds it, the safety pass fixes it).

zones_clean_how.overview: The centerpiece of the chapter, Zone by Zone: Exactly How to Clean It. Each zone gets the same three things: the inputs to gather, the numbered steps in the order you actually do them, and what to inspect and flag while your hands are already there. Gather the inputs into your caddy before you start, so you are not walking off mid-clean to fetch a cloth. Every procedure is the universal nine-rule Shine method applied to a particular zone, in the true order of work: clear, dust high and dry, glass, surfaces, details, floor last.

zone_1_landing_spot.surfaces: The tray, the console top, the mirror or art above it, the wall and switch plate beside the door, the charging dock, and the floor beneath. Keys shed grit and coins leave a grey film, so the film under the tray tells you how long it has been since anyone did this properly.
zone_1_landing_spot.inputs: Streak-free glass and mirror cleaner; neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; floor-material-compatible cleaner matched to your floor; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (one glass cloth, one surface cloth, one dry buffing cloth, one floor cloth); a small soft detail brush; a compact vacuum with the crevice tool fitted; a portable caddy.
zone_1_landing_spot.steps: 1) Clear and unplug (take everything off, lift the tray out, remove the paper folder, unplug the charging dock before any damp cloth comes near it). 2) Dust high and dry, first (the mirror or frame top edge and the console back edge where dust packs into the seam). 3) Do the mirror or glass (mist the glass cleaner onto the glass cloth, wipe one direction, buff dry in the crossing direction). 4) Wipe the wall and switch plate (lift finger marks and scuffs, gently on painted plaster, dry behind you). 5) Clean the console top (mist onto the surface cloth, work back edge to front, give sticky rings a few seconds, then dry with the buffing cloth). 6) Wash the tray (wipe the grey film ring, wash the tray inside and out, detail brush into the corners, dry fully before the keys go back). 7) Clean the dock and cable, dry only (dock unplugged, dry or barely damp cloth, dry detail brush through the port and along the cable, coil loosely). 8) Do the floor, last (vacuum the grit with the crevice tool, then mop the sealed floor and let it dry).
zone_1_landing_spot.inspect_and_flag: A brown water ring or spreading stain under the hooks; a cracked, frayed, or hardened charging cable, or a plug with a scorch mark or that sits warm; a warm or yellowed power strip; a console leg or wall bracket that rocks; green or white crust on the dock's metal contacts. Flag each and keep cleaning; the safety pass fixes them.

zone_2_coats_and_outerwear.surfaces: The shelf above the rail, the hat and glove bin, the rail and hooks, the shoulders of the hanging coats, the wall behind the hooks, the umbrella stand, and the floor beneath. Work from the shelf down.
zone_2_coats_and_outerwear.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth, a floor cloth); a compact vacuum with the soft upholstery brush and the crevice tool; a small detail brush for the umbrella stand; a portable caddy.
zone_2_coats_and_outerwear.steps: 1) Take the bin down and empty it (shake it out, contents on a clean surface, not the floor). 2) Dust the shelf, then wipe it (reach the back edge and the front lip where a grey line settles above eye level). 3) Clean the bin, inside and out (dry fully before hats and gloves go back, because wool put away damp starts a musty smell). 4) Brush the coats (shoulders and collars downward with the soft upholstery tool or a dry brush). 5) Wipe the rail and hooks (slide the coats along, wipe the rail full length and each hook and base plate, dry the rail so nothing rusts). 6) Wipe the wall behind the hooks (lift the dark scuff, gently on painted plaster, dry after). 7) Empty and scrub the umbrella stand (tip out water and grit, scrub inside with cleaner and the detail brush, rinse, stand it upside down to dry). 8) Do the floor, last (vacuum under the hanging line and behind the stand, then mop the sealed floor).
zone_2_coats_and_outerwear.inspect_and_flag: A hook base plate pulling away from the wall; a rail bracket with a screw backing out, or a bowing rail; a brown damp bloom or soft patch on the wall behind soaked coats; a musty mildew smell off a coat or the bin; rust or a crack in the umbrella stand. Flag each and keep going.

zone_3_shoes_and_boots.surfaces: The rack shelves, the footwear, the boot tray, the wall and skirting behind the rack, the floor under the rack, and the clear strip between the door and the rack. The boot tray takes longer than you expect, and it is the whole point: its salt and grit is what scratches every floor in the house.
zone_3_shoes_and_boots.inputs: Floor-material-compatible cleaner; neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a floor cloth); a stiff dry brush for caked mud and the boot tray; a compact vacuum with the crevice tool; access to an outside tap or a hose for the boot tray; a portable caddy.
zone_3_shoes_and_boots.steps: 1) Clear the rack and knock off the mud (outside, knock soles together and brush caked mud off the welts with the stiff dry brush). 2) Wipe the shoes you keep (uppers of the pairs that live on the rack; shake and wipe the slippers' soles). 3) Wipe the rack shelves (knock loose dried mud into the bin, wipe front to back, dry them). 4) Take the boot tray outside and wash it (hose it, scrub the salt film and grit from the corners with the stiff brush and cleaner, rinse, dry fully before it comes back). 5) Wipe the wall and skirting (lift mud spray and scuff, barely damp, dry after). 6) Vacuum under the rack (the grit trap in the dark underneath, then wipe the sealed floor there). 7) Do the clear floor strip, last (vacuum the full stride-wide strip, then mop it and let it dry).
zone_3_shoes_and_boots.inspect_and_flag: A hairline crack or split in the boot tray, and any dark stain under it; a sagging rack shelf or a loose joint so the rack rocks; rust on the metal frame where salt water pools; a damp stain or soft patch on the skirting; the floor finish worn dull, grey, or rough under the tray. Flag each.

zone_4_bench_or_console.surfaces: The wall and back edge, the console top, the seat, the drawer taken fully out, the runners and cavity, the drawer fronts and legs, and the floor beneath. The seat collects the same grit as the floor, because people sit on it in outdoor clothes. Work top down, back to front.
zone_4_bench_or_console.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a dry cloth, a floor cloth); a compact vacuum with the upholstery tool and the crevice tool; a small detail brush for the drawer corners; a portable caddy.
zone_4_bench_or_console.steps: 1) Clear the top and take the drawer out (top to three items or fewer, pull the drawer out of its runners, lift out any divider). 2) Wipe the wall and back edge (clear the dust line where the top meets the wall). 3) Clean the top (dust or vacuum, then wipe the whole surface and dry it). 4) Do the seat (vacuum the seat and its seams with the upholstery tool, wipe a hard seat or spot-clean a padded one, let it dry). 5) Clean the drawer (tip sand and crumbs from the back corners, wipe the base and sections, detail brush into the corners, wipe the divider). 6) Wipe the runners and vacuum the cavity (both runner tracks, and the grit that has dropped behind the drawer). 7) Wipe the fronts and legs (the handles and the kick line at the bottom). 8) Do the floor, last (vacuum under and around the legs, then mop the sealed floor).
zone_4_bench_or_console.inspect_and_flag: A console that rocks or tips when you lean on the top; a drawer runner screw backing out so the drawer drops or drags; a hairline split in the seat or a lifting splinter on a wooden bench; a wobble in a leg joint or a cracked or seized caster; a water ring or swelling on the top. Flag each.

zone_5_door_mat_and_immediate_floor.surfaces: The door face and frame, the handle and letterbox and any glass panel, the bottom edge and threshold, the inside mat, the outside coarse mat, and the floor inside the swing. Honestly, the mat is most of the job, because it is the one thing standing between the outside and every other floor in the house.
zone_5_door_mat_and_immediate_floor.inputs: Neutral pH multi-surface cleaner; streak-free glass and mirror cleaner, if the door has a glass panel; floor-material-compatible cleaner; a colour-coded microfiber cloth set (a surface cloth, a glass cloth, a dry cloth, a floor cloth); a compact vacuum with the crevice tool; access to an outside space to beat and wash the mats; a portable caddy.
zone_5_door_mat_and_immediate_floor.steps: 1) Dust the top rail and clear the corners (dust the door top rail, clear cobwebs from the frame corners). 2) Wipe the door face, top to bottom (extra attention to the panels and the kick line at the base). 3) Wipe the frame and architrave (the top ledge and the strike-side edge hands push against). 4) Clean the handle, letterbox, and glass (wipe the handle and flap; for glass, mist the glass cloth, wipe one direction, buff dry). 5) Clean the bottom edge and threshold (open the door, run a damp cloth along the bottom edge and threshold strip, lift the dark grit line, dry after). 6) Vacuum, beat, and wash the inside mat (top face, flip and vacuum the underside, then beat it outdoors and wash it if washable; return it only fully dry). 7) Shake out the outside mat (beat the grit and salt out, hose the rubber-backed sort, stand it to dry). 8) Do the floor inside the swing, last (both mats up, vacuum the whole patch including where the mats sat, then mop and let it dry).
zone_5_door_mat_and_immediate_floor.inspect_and_flag: A curled mat or backing gone brittle and shedding crumbs; a dropped hinge so the door scrapes, or a loose hinge screw; a swelling, dark line, or soft patch along the door bottom or threshold; a door that no longer latches on the first push, or a squashed threshold seal; a water stain spreading just inside the threshold. Flag each.

the_room_and_the_playbook.the_room: The throughline space is the entryway, decomposed into its five zones: the landing spot (the tray and the paper), the coats (the rail and the hooks), the shoes (the rack and the grit they carry), the bench or console (the seat and its drawer), and the door with its mat and the small stretch of floor inside its swing. You can run the zones in any order, but within each one the loop runs in the same fixed sequence, and the deep, detailed part of it, the part this chapter is really about, is Shine. If you want the biggest visible win first, start with the landing spot, the entryway's single highest-leverage square foot.

the_quick_passes.note: Before the deep clean, four of the other five passes are quick, so the chapter moves through them briskly and then slows right down for Shine, which is where the real work is.
the_quick_passes.sort: Sort each zone first, because you cannot clean a surface that is covered. Empty it, and let nothing back without a verdict: keys and today's coat and this week's shoes stay; the dead batteries, odd gloves, purposeless paper, and split-soled trainers go to the out box.
the_quick_passes.straighten: Straighten what survives into a home chosen by use: the tray where your hand opens, hooks for daily coats, the lowest hook at the shortest person's height, boots in the tray, two mats and no more. Those two passes clear the ground so the clean can happen.
the_quick_passes.safety_standardize_sustain: Safety, Standardize, and Sustain come after the shine, and each is short. Safety acts on everything the cleaning turned up (anchor the tippy console, take the overloaded strip out of the drip line, replace the frayed cable you flagged). Standardize locks the result (photograph the finished landing spot and tape it inside the cupboard, name each shoe shelf, tape the mat outline). Sustain hangs the upkeep on things that already happen (coat off, hands full, everything into the tray; dishwasher on, console back to three; bin night, the boot tray goes out).

the_room_and_the_playbook.how_to_shine_the_method: Shine is where a room stops being tidy and becomes clean, and it is the pass most people do worst, because they were never taught a method. There is one, it is not complicated, and it is the same in every zone and every room in the book: learn it once here and use it in all nineteen chapters that follow. The Shine method, frozen: Shine is cleaning to a method, not wiping until it looks better: work top to bottom and dry before wet, mist the cloth and not the surface, clean with one cloth and dry with a second, and let your eye inspect every surface your hand passes over; you leave the zone genuinely clean, and you find what needs fixing on the way. The nine rules the method rests on (each zone procedure is just these applied to a particular zone): work top to bottom; work dry before wet; work back to front, clean to dirty; mist the cloth, not the surface; use two cloths, one to clean and one to dry; colour-code your cloths and never use fabric softener; match the cleaner to the surface; give the cleaner a moment to work; and clean to inspect, and flag, do not fix (Shine finds it, the safety pass fixes it).
the_room_and_the_playbook.zone_by_zone_exactly_how_to_clean_it: The core of the chapter. Each zone gets the same three things: the inputs to gather into the caddy before you start, the numbered steps in the order you actually do them (clear, dust high and dry, glass, surfaces, details, floor last), and what to inspect and flag while your hands are already there. See the zones_clean_how object for the full per-zone inputs, steps, and inspect-and-flag lists for Zone 1 the landing spot, Zone 2 the coats and outerwear, Zone 3 the shoes and boots, Zone 4 the bench or console, and Zone 5 the door, mat, and immediate floor.

the_calls_that_matter.note: Cleaning to a method will make the room shine, but three genuinely hard decisions decide whether it stays clear enough to keep clean, and a playbook earns its keep by naming them.
the_calls_that_matter.the_paper: The first is the paper on the landing spot. Nothing returns to the surface without a verdict, and there are only three: act, file, or recycle. A sheet that has sat more than fourteen days has stopped being paperwork and become a decision, so do it tonight or recycle it. Both are answers; leaving it on the surface is not.
the_calls_that_matter.the_guilty_coat: The second is the coat you feel guilty about. Coats are counted by weather, not by number; each person gets one coat per kind of weather your climate genuinely produces, and a second in the same category has to beat the first on a specific, nameable day. The expensive coat you never wear is not exempt, because the money is already spent whether it hangs here or keeps someone else warm.
the_calls_that_matter.the_tired_mat: The third is the mat, which wears out while looking perfectly fine, so you test it instead of looking at it. Walk in on a dry, gritty day, wipe your feet the way you actually do, then lift the mat and look at both the floor beneath it and the fibres. If the grit is sitting on top and walking straight off, replace it this month, because a worn mat is quietly sanding the finish off every floor between the front door and the kitchen.

the_room_and_the_playbook.watch_for_at_the_door: Cleaning to inspect will surface most of the room's hazards for you, but run the five safety questions once directly, so nothing is missed, and act here on everything the clean flagged. Water and electricity: keep the charging dock and any power strip out of the drip line below the wet umbrellas and sleeves. Burn or fire: never chain a dock, a lamp, and a plug-in heater to one strip; one dock, one outlet, nothing chained. Poison, choke, or strangle: keep long scarves and bag straps off the low hooks at a child's neck height, and loose button batteries, coins, and magnets out of a low drawer and into a lidded tin. Fall, cut, or crush: anchor a tippy console or a top-heavy shoe rack and keep the heavy things low. And the plain fall: keep the stride of floor inside the door clear, and the mat flat and gripped.
the_room_and_the_playbook.before_and_after: Here is the ritual that closes every room in Part 9. When the five zones are done and cleaned to the method, stand where you stood at the start, just inside the door, and take the second photograph. Shoot it as a true matched pair: one chosen spot just inside the door at standing height, framing the landing spot and the coats together, before and after, same angle and same light, and do not tidy before the before. The before is the valuable one, the proof of how far the room came; the after is the standard, the ideal-state photo from Standardize, and taping it inside the cupboard turns keeping the entryway nice into a specific target anyone can check in a glance. That is the entryway: five small zones, each sorted, homed, and cleaned to a professional method, its hazards flagged and fixed, and a photo pair to hold it. The door is done, and genuinely clean.

definition: A finished entryway is one where everyone can land and launch in seconds: keys and phone drop into one tray, today's coat and shoes have an easy home, wet things stay on the mat, and the paper that comes through the door leaves again with a verdict. Nothing lives on the floor inside the door's swing, and two hooks always stand empty for whoever arrives next.
rule: You do not 6S a whole room. You 6S one zone of it, then the next, until the room is done. A room is only ever a handful of small zones wearing a single name, and a zone is a job you can finish in an afternoon.
the_five_zones: The entryway is five small zones, not one big job: the landing spot where pockets empty, the coats, the shoes, the bench or console, and the door with its mat and the strip of floor inside its swing. Do them one at a time and the room takes a few short sessions, not a lost weekend.
first_and_last_reframe: The entryway is the room you spend the least time in and notice the most, because you cross it every single time you come or go. A calm doorway is the first thing that greets you home and the last thing that speeds you out, which is why the smallest room in the house pays back a 6S loop faster than any other room you own.
count_by_weather_reframe: Coats are counted by weather, not by number. Each person gets one coat per kind of weather your climate genuinely produces, and a second in the same category has to beat the first on a specific, nameable day. The expensive coat you never wear is not exempt, because the money is already spent whether it hangs here or keeps someone else warm.
worn_mat_reframe: A mat looks perfectly fine long after it has stopped working, so you test it instead of looking at it. A finished mat sits with its fibres flattened one way and the grit rides straight over it onto the next pair of shoes. A worn mat is not saving you anything, it is quietly sanding the finish off every floor between the front door and the kitchen.

callouts.quick_win: Do one zone, start to finish, to the method: gather the inputs into your caddy, clear the surface, then work top to bottom, dry before wet, clean cloth then dry cloth, and finish with the floor. The landing spot takes about twenty minutes and is the entryway's single highest-leverage square foot. You will feel the difference the next time you walk in.
callouts.family_challenge: Everyone claims their own named shoe shelf and their own hook, with the lowest hook set at the shortest person's height, and two hooks left empty for whoever visits. A third pair or a stray coat then has visibly nowhere to go, and nobody has to nag, because the empty hook does the asking.
callouts.sixs_tip: Colour-code your cloths and never wash them with fabric softener. One colour for glass, one for surfaces, one for the floor and the boot tray, so you never carry grit or grime from a dirty surface onto a clean one. Softener coats the fibres and destroys the grab that makes microfiber work, so it wipes like a wet rag instead.
callouts.common_mistake: Wiping until it looks better instead of cleaning to a method. Skipping the dry-dust-first step so you smear grit into mud, spraying cleaner straight onto a mirror so it runs behind the frame, leaving a wet floor to streak and slip, using one grey cloth for everything so you move dirt from the boot tray to the console. The method exists because it is faster and it actually works. Follow the order.

one_idea_to_keep: A zone is not clean because it looks clean. It is clean because you gathered the right inputs, took it apart, and cleaned every surface to a method, top to bottom, dry before wet, one cloth to clean and one to dry, inspecting as you went. Do that to one zone this weekend, and let the door start working for you every time you cross it.
before_and_after_caption: This is the entryway the whole loop was for: the same doorway you started with, cleared, calmed, and holding only what the door actually needs. Take the before photo before you touch a thing, because within a month you will not believe the room was ever the other one, and take the after photo as the standard, because it is the picture the door has to match from now on.

The friction meter reached its goal at Chapter 30 (SUSTAIN COMPLETE, all six S's) and is RETIRED for Part 9. Its recurring-close role is now carried by a matched before-and-after pair of the same entryway spot, shot from just inside the door at adult standing height, plus the two photos to take: the before (kept, per Chapter 6, the valuable one, private proof of how far the room has come) and the after (the ideal-state standard, per Chapter 25, taped inside the coat cupboard as the picture the door has to match). This is the new recurring ritual for Chapters 31 to 50, and it gives every room its own concrete transformation. The frozen before-and-after caption governs the figure. There is no friction-meter figure in this chapter or in any Part 9 chapter
